In @fig-12-stopping-envelope-phase-plane, the gap between the inset boundary and the braking-only curve is the clearance consumed by pre-brake delay, the matched stop's jerk ramps, and the fixed allowances, and it is the gap that sets the speed ceiling.

Just as the Roofline model [@williams2009roofline] caps attainable computing throughput by memory bandwidth in memory-bound regimes, the stopping envelope establishes a **Kinematic Roofline** on the physical system: available physical clearance ($D_{\text{clear}}$) caps legal transit velocity, regardless of how quickly the upstream policy computes or how many TOPS of neural acceleration are hosted on the system-on-chip (SoC). When an autonomous system operates in a clearance-bound regime, a higher inference rate buys no speed at all. Model size and inference speed matter only through latency, which enters $\tau_{\text{delay}}$: on this machine every `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.tick_ms_str` of added delay costs `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.missed_tick_str` of clearance at the aisle speed, and 10 ms more delay lowers the ceiling by about `{python} EnforcementStoppingBudget.ceiling_drop_10ms_str` mm/s. A larger model that adds latency therefore lowers the ceiling, and a faster one raises it only slightly. The ceiling moves materially only with the physical terms: credible braking deceleration $a_{\text{brake}}$, transport lag $\tau_{\text{delay}}$, the tracking bound $\epsilon_{\text{track}}$, and localization uncertainty $\delta_{\text{loc}}$.

These parameters are not stationary. An item in the gripper raises the arm's inertia and lowers the deceleration its joints can produce within peak torque, oil on the floor lowers the traction beneath the base's credible deceleration, and repeated hard stops heat rotors and inverters into thermal derating\index{Thermal derating} (@sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles). An enforcer that treats $a_{\text{brake}}$ as a datasheet constant underestimates the envelope precisely under heavy load, so it must use independently bounded braking capability and reduce permitted speed when validated friction, payload, or thermal conditions change; an uncertain estimate cannot by itself restore a guarantee.

Adaptation works only while the enforcer's state estimates are accurate and the actuators can still supply the force. If contamination takes traction toward zero or a sustained duty cycle pushes the windings past their ceilings, the assumed deceleration vanishes, and once the required torque exceeds what the hardware can produce, the enforcer can detect the violation but can no longer prevent it.

## Authority Exhaustion and Emergency Fallback {#sec-enforcement-exhausted-authority}

A loaded arm descending toward the packing station must counter gravity before any torque remains to slow its motion. **Actuator saturation**\index{Actuator!saturation} occurs when the requested effort reaches the electrical, mechanical, or thermal limits of the body (@sec-body-actuator-limits); integral control can then accumulate windup\index{Controller!windup}. When motor phase currents hit inverter current-chopping limits ($I_{\max}$), the DC voltage rail sags under heavy inductive transients ($L dI/dt$), back-EMF at high rotor speeds collapses available voltage headroom ($V_{\text{rail}} - K_e \omega \to 0$), or winding temperatures approach thermal derating thresholds ($T_j \to T_{\max}$, @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles), the corrective control action $\mathbf{u}_{\text{corr}}$ cannot be delivered at its commanded magnitude. No mathematical boundary can be protected with force the physical body cannot generate.

If the required braking effort exceeds the actuator limits, no filter can recover the promised stop. The permission path must select a surviving response, but a response selected after this loss can limit harm without restoring the lost guarantee. The reservation therefore has to contract before the available braking effort is exhausted.

A stopping envelope\index{Stopping envelope} based on peak torque alone can overstate braking authority when gravity drives the moving load toward the hazard.[^fn-math-margin-loss] Under a steady-state bias torque $\tau_{\text{bias}}$, the effective deceleration available to arrest angular motion collapses:
$$\alpha_{\text{net}} = \frac{\tau_{\max} - \tau_{\text{bias}}}{J}$$ {#eq-enforce-effective-deceleration}
where $J$ is mechanism inertia and $\tau_{\max}$ is the peak dynamic torque limit. In linear translational systems with mass $m$ and bias force $u_{\text{bias}}$, @eq-enforce-effective-deceleration takes the equivalent form $a_{\text{net}} = (u_{\max} - |u_{\text{bias}}|) / m$. For motion in the direction of the bias, a load consuming three-quarters of peak opposing torque leaves one-quarter for net braking, quadrupling the constant-deceleration distance at the same speed.

Crucially, gravitational and dynamic bias is directionally asymmetric. When motion is against gravity (such as during an upward arm swing), gravitational bias assists motor braking, yielding $\alpha_{\text{net}} = (\tau_{\max} + \tau_{\text{bias}}) / J$. Conversely, when moving in the direction of the bias (a descending arm carrying a payload toward a workstation), gravity opposes deceleration, collapsing braking headroom to $\alpha_{\text{net}} = (\tau_{\max} - \tau_{\text{bias}}) / J$. Because safety certificates must guarantee forward invariance in the worst-case physical direction, the enforcer must evaluate $\alpha_{\text{net}}$ with directional sign awareness, rather than treating braking authority as an isotropic scalar.

[^fn-math-margin-loss]: **Actuator bias torque and stopping margin loss**\index{Actuator!Bias torque}\index{Stopping envelope!Margin loss}: When gravity drives motion toward the hazard, the motor must oppose that bias as well as decelerate the load. The example uses a bias equal to three-quarters of peak opposing torque, leaving one-quarter as net braking headroom. Bias of the opposite sign can assist braking. For a detailed derivation of saturated authority and stopping margin contraction, see @sec-appendix-control-cbf.

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-authority-loss
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ AUTHORITY LOSS ON THE MACHINE: ARM BIAS TORQUE AND BASE WINDUP
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the descending-arm and windup paragraphs immediately below;
# │          reused by calc-enforcement-kinetic-barrier.
# │ Goal:    show that bias torque quarters the arm's braking and that windup
# │          delay on the base overruns the spare.
# │ Show:    arm stop with and without bias; unbraked windup travel vs. spare.
# │ How:     RM.arm.max_torque, RM.tcp_speed_limit, AISLE fields,
# │          calc_scurve_stop_distance for the finished budget at the aisle
# │          speed (jerk bound from calc_c2_stop_suffix at the drive limit).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import math
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_c2_stop_suffix, calc_scurve_stop_distance
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, fmt_torque, fmt_inertia, fmt_percent, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementAuthorityLoss:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    torque_limit = RM.arm.max_torque  # category: datasheet (peak torque, axes 1-4)
    tcp_limit = RM.tcp_speed_limit  # category: chosen
    inertia = 3.0 * kilogram * meter**2  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative (joint with payload)
    link_length = 0.80 * meter  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    joint_speed = 1.2 / second  # rad/s; scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    bias_fraction = 0.75  # scenario assumption; share of peak torque holding the load on descent; category: illustrative
    windup_span = 200 * millisecond  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    unwind = 150 * millisecond  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived
    fixed_overhead = AISLE.fixed_overhead  # category: illustrative + chosen
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    bias = (torque_limit * bias_fraction).to(newton * meter)
    net_torque = (torque_limit - bias).to(newton * meter)
    alpha_nom = (torque_limit / inertia).to(1 / second**2)
    alpha_eff = (net_torque / inertia).to(1 / second**2)
    angle_nom = (joint_speed**2 / (2 * alpha_nom)).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    angle_eff = (joint_speed**2 / (2 * alpha_eff)).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    d_nom = (link_length * angle_nom).to(millimeter)
    d_eff = (link_length * angle_eff).to(millimeter)
    overrun = (d_eff - d_nom).to(millimeter)
    tcp_speed = (link_length * joint_speed).to(meter / second)
    windup_travel = (v_aisle * unwind).to(millimeter)
    j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(RM.base.max_velocity, a_brake)["peak_jerk"]  # reference polynomial's peak jerk
    budget = (v_aisle * tau_delay + calc_scurve_stop_distance(v_aisle, a_brake, j_brake) + fixed_overhead).to(millimeter)
    spare = (d_clear - budget).to(millimeter)
    windup_excess = (windup_travel - spare).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(bias.magnitude - 65.25) < 1e-9, "Bias is 65.25 of 87 N·m.")
    check(abs(alpha_nom.magnitude / alpha_eff.magnitude - 4.0) < 1e-9, "Bias quarters the braking deceleration.")
    check(abs(d_eff.magnitude / d_nom.magnitude - 4.0) < 1e-9, "Bias quadruples the tool stopping travel.")
    check(tcp_speed <= tcp_limit, "The descending tool point stays inside the free-space TCP limit.")
    check(abs(windup_travel.magnitude - 195.0) < 1e-9, "Windup at 1.3 m/s adds 195 mm.")
    check(abs(spare.magnitude - 131.0075) < 1e-6, "The finished budget leaves 131.01 mm spare at 1.3 m/s.")
    check(windup_travel > spare, "Windup travel exceeds the spare.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    torque_limit_str = fmt_torque(torque_limit, precision=0)
    bias_str = fmt_torque(bias, precision=2)
    net_torque_str = fmt_torque(net_torque, precision=2)
    bias_pct_str = fmt_percent(bias_fraction, precision=0, style="prose")
    inertia_str = fmt_inertia(inertia, precision=0)
    link_length_str = fmt_length(link_length, unit=meter, precision=2)
    joint_speed_str = fmt(joint_speed.magnitude, precision=1)
    tcp_speed_str = fmt_velocity(tcp_speed, precision=2)
    tcp_limit_str = fmt_velocity(tcp_limit, precision=0)
    alpha_nom_str = fmt(alpha_nom.magnitude, precision=0)
    alpha_eff_str = fmt(alpha_eff.magnitude, precision=2)
    angle_nom_str = fmt(angle_nom, precision=4)
    angle_eff_str = fmt(angle_eff, precision=4)
    angle_nom_deg_str = fmt(math.degrees(angle_nom), precision=2)
    angle_eff_deg_str = fmt(math.degrees(angle_eff), precision=2)
    d_nom_str = fmt_length(d_nom, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    d_eff_str = fmt_length(d_eff, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    overrun_str = fmt_length(overrun, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    windup_span_str = fmt_latency(windup_span, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    unwind_str = fmt_latency(unwind, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(v_aisle, precision=1)
    windup_travel_str = fmt_length(windup_travel, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    windup_excess_str = fmt_length(windup_excess, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    spare_str = fmt_length(spare, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
```

Consider the warehouse mobile manipulator's arm carrying the mug from the takeaway conveyor down toward the coworker at the packing station, with the loaded joint descending at an angular velocity $\omega_0 =$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.joint_speed_str` $\text{rad/s}$ (the scenario's values are illustrative; see the Reader Guide). The effective link length is $\ell =$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.link_length_str`, so the tool point moves at `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.tcp_speed_str`, inside the arm's `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.tcp_limit_str` free-space limit; only the final approach to the coworker's hand runs at the far lower handover speed that @sec-enforcement-telemetry records. The joint inertia with the mug is $J =$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.inertia_str`, and the joint's peak torque is $\tau_{\max} =$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.torque_limit_str`. With no gravitational bias ($\tau_{\text{bias}} = 0$), the whole peak torque is available for braking, and the angular deceleration is $\alpha_{\text{nom}} = \tau_{\max}/J =$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.alpha_nom_str` $\text{rad/s}^2$. The stopping angle from $\omega_0$ is $\Delta \theta_{\text{nom}} = \omega_0^2 / (2 \alpha_{\text{nom}}) =$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.angle_nom_str` $\text{rad}$ (`{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.angle_nom_deg_str`$^\circ$), which moves the tool point $d_{\text{tool,nom}} = \ell \Delta \theta_{\text{nom}} =$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.d_nom_str` along its arc.

During the descent, however, the arm's own geometry and the mug load the joint with a downward bias of $\tau_{\text{bias}} =$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.bias_str`, `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.bias_pct_str` of its peak torque. By @eq-enforce-effective-deceleration, the net torque left for braking is $\tau_{\max} - \tau_{\text{bias}} =$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.net_torque_str`, and the angular deceleration falls fourfold to $\alpha_{\text{net}} =$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.alpha_eff_str` $\text{rad/s}^2$. The stopping angle grows fourfold to `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.angle_eff_str` $\text{rad}$ (`{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.angle_eff_deg_str`$^\circ$), and the tool travels `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.d_eff_str`, an unbudgeted overrun of `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.overrun_str`. If the enforcer evaluates barrier envelopes with the datasheet torque $\tau_{\max}$ rather than the net headroom $\tau_{\max} - \tau_{\text{bias}}$, the real stop runs `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.overrun_str` past the predicted one. Whether that overrun ends on the station surface depends on the clearance at which braking begins, which the barrier of @sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission evaluates. The coworker's hand must never come within the arm's biased stop of `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.d_eff_str` plus its blind travel before the handover channel engages.

An unprotected integrator beneath the enforcer can add latency during saturation. In the illustrative controller failure considered here, clipping does not stop integration, and the brake request passes through the same wound-up controller instead of bypassing or resetting it. The output consequently remains at the forward limit while the integral unwinds. If error accumulates for `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.windup_span_str`, unwinding delays net braking force by $\tau_{\text{unwind}} =$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.unwind_str`. On the mobile manipulator's base at the `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.v_aisle_str` aisle speed, this delay adds $v\,\tau_{\text{unwind}} =$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.windup_travel_str` of unbraked travel, `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.windup_excess_str` more than even the `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.spare_str` unallocated remainder before dispatch-to-admission travel is charged. Anti-windup clamping, back-calculation, and conditional integration address the loop [@astrom2006advanced; @franklin1998digital]; the enforcement requirement is to measure the unwinding delay that remains and budget its unbraked distance inside the stopping horizon.

Saturation is one of the few hardware failures with a direct, deterministic detector inside the permission path. On each $1\text{ ms}$ tick the permission path compares the commanded effort $u_{\text{cmd}}$ with the realizable effort $u_{\text{act}} = \text{clip}(u_{\text{cmd}}, u_{\text{min}}, u_{\text{max}})$. A nonzero difference or current-limit status reports clipping of the requested effort. This is a direct detector of commanded saturation, not a measurement of delivered torque or tire traction. Current, voltage, thermal, and state evidence still bound the physical braking authority.

Because consumed authority changes the stopping distance at once, the enforcer folds it into the envelope in real time, recomputing $a_{\text{net}} = (u_{\text{max}} - |u_{\text{bias}}|) / m$ before verifying the next trajectory segment. The allowable speed falls as authority is consumed, and when the computed stop no longer fits inside the clear distance, the enforcer must command deceleration while enough authority remains.

Authority depletion must also reach the planner. A `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.chunk_rate_hz_str` $\text{Hz}$ policy that keeps commanding accelerations to a motor the `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.loop_rate_str` loop has reported saturated is planning against a body that cannot execute them, so the permission path reports saturation as an active constraint violation, revokes the active trajectory, and requires a re-plan from the machine's authority-constrained state.

::: {#psp-enforcement-actuator-authority .callout-perspective title="The actuator authority invariant"}
A Control Barrier Function\index{Control barrier function}, as formulated in @sec-appendix-control-cbf, is mathematically valid only while physical actuators retain sufficient current, voltage, and thermal headroom to deliver the computed corrective force: $u^* \in [u_{\min}, u_{\max}]$. When steady-state gravity or friction consumes the actuator's operating envelope, the enforcer must dynamically contract the safe set before control authority at the margin vanishes.
:::

::: {#chk-enforce-actuator-saturation-headroom .callout-checkpoint title="Stopping envelope and actuator headroom"}

Consider how the stopping envelope, and the actuator authority beneath it, bound permissible motion:

- [ ] **Quadratic envelope scaling**: Can you explain why the stopping budget grows faster than speed, so that the finished budget, rather than the drive limit, sets the aisle speed, and why no planning policy can bypass this kinematic floor?
- [ ] **Transport lag vs. braking power**: Can you distinguish between the spatial cost of computational transport delay ($v \cdot \tau_{\text{delay}}$) and active braking ($v^2 / 2 a_{\text{brake}}$), identifying which term dominates at low crawling speeds vs. high transit speeds?
- [ ] **Effective deceleration collapse**: Can you describe the physical mechanism that causes stopping distance to quadruple when steady-state gravity consumes 75 percent of peak actuator torque?
- [ ] **Dynamic safe set contraction**: Can you explain why the permission path must actively shrink the admissible state space when an actuator approaches thermal or electrical saturation, rather than waiting for tracking error to breach a hard limit?
:::

## Safe Sets as Conditional Permission {#sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission}

Once its bias torque is counted, the descending arm of @sec-enforcement-exhausted-authority needs `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.d_eff_str` of tool travel to stop, and that travel grows with the square of approach speed. A clearance that suffices at one speed is therefore too short at a higher one, and the enforcer needs a predicate over position and speed together that it can evaluate on every tick of the control clock.

The stopping budget already defines a physical margin. A control barrier function turns that margin into a restriction on the next command [@ames2014control; @ames2019control]; it is one member of the family of **safety filters** that monitor a proposal against a fallback and override it only when needed [@hsu2024safetyfilter], so the machine can continue approaching while retaining enough authority to stop.

A **safe set**\index{Safe set} collects the states for which a scalar certificate remains nonnegative. Its boundary has zero margin; its interior has positive margin. For the arm, position and speed must both enter the certificate because the same position can admit a slow approach and reject a fast one:
$$\mathcal{C} = \{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X} \mid h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0\}, \quad \partial \mathcal{C} = \{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X} \mid h(\mathbf{x}) = 0\}, \quad \text{Int}(\mathcal{C}) = \{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X} \mid h(\mathbf{x}) > 0\}.$$
Forward invariance of $\mathcal{C}$ is the physical counterpart to an **inductive loop invariant**:
$$h(\mathbf{x}_0) \ge 0 \quad \land \quad \dot{h}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}) \ge -\kappa(h(\mathbf{x})) \quad \implies \quad h(\mathbf{x}_t) \ge 0 \quad \forall t \ge 0.$$
The implication is a continuous-time result under the model and feasibility assumptions. Nagumo's theorem [@blanchini1999set] supplies the boundary interpretation: motion at the boundary must point tangent to or into the set. The rate function $\kappa(\cdot)$, an extended class-$\mathcal{K}$ function, increases with margin and vanishes at zero, allowing faster approach deep inside the set and requiring nondecreasing margin at its boundary. Sampling, uncertain state, and delayed torque delivery require additional margins before this argument can describe a physical implementation.

### Kinetic barrier certificates and relative degree {#sec-enforcement-kinetic-barrier-certificates}

At the causal boundary, software proposals encounter continuous physical dynamics governed by the control-affine differential equation:
$$\dot{\mathbf{x}} = f(\mathbf{x}) + g(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u}$$
where $f(\mathbf{x})$ captures unforced physical drift (inertia, Coriolis forces, gravitational bias, and passive rolling friction), $g(\mathbf{x})$ maps control inputs to instantaneous acceleration, and $\mathbf{u}$ represents the joint torque the drives deliver. On this machine the drives close the current and velocity loops, so the MCU never writes $\mathbf{u}$ directly; stage 5 of @sec-enforcement-loop-budget shows how a torque-space decision reaches the drive as a setpoint. Evaluating how a scalar safety barrier certificate $h(\mathbf{x})$ evolves across this boundary requires computing its directional time derivative along system trajectories:
$$\dot{h}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}) = \nabla h(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \dot{\mathbf{x}} = \underbrace{\nabla h(\mathbf{x}) \cdot f(\mathbf{x})}_{L_f h(\mathbf{x})} + \underbrace{\left(\nabla h(\mathbf{x}) \cdot g(\mathbf{x})\right)}_{L_g h(\mathbf{x})} \mathbf{u}$$
In nonlinear control literature, $L_f h$ and $L_g h$ are traditionally called Lie derivatives. In modern computational terms, these directional derivatives are simply **Jacobian-vector products (JVPs)**, familiar from automatic differentiation engines (such as JAX or PyTorch):
$$L_f h(\mathbf{x}) = \nabla h(\mathbf{x})^\top f(\mathbf{x}) = \text{JVP}(h, \mathbf{x}, f(\mathbf{x})), \qquad L_g h(\mathbf{x}) = \nabla h(\mathbf{x})^\top g(\mathbf{x}) = \text{JVP}(h, \mathbf{x}, g(\mathbf{x})).$$
In forward-mode automatic differentiation, a JVP evaluates the directional derivative along one tangent vector. When $g$ has several input columns $g_j$, the notation $\operatorname{JVP}(h,\mathbf{x},g)$ above means the row of separate products $\operatorname{JVP}(h,\mathbf{x},g_j)$, one per input channel; the matrix itself is not a single tangent vector. The drift product and these control-channel products have distinct physical meanings:

1. $L_f h(\mathbf{x}) = \text{JVP}(h, \mathbf{x}, f(\mathbf{x}))$ is the **system drift JVP**—the rate at which the safety margin diminishes purely from the robot's physical momentum, gravitational bias, and passive environmental dynamics.
2. $L_g h(\mathbf{x}) = \text{JVP}(h, \mathbf{x}, g(\mathbf{x}))$ is the **control authority JVP**—the instantaneous gradient sensitivity that commanded motor torque exerts over the rate of barrier change across the causal boundary.

Formulating an effective Control Barrier Function requires navigating the **relative degree trap**\index{Relative degree!relative degree trap}. In compiler and graph terms, relative degree represents the graph distance (number of integrator nodes) between the commanded control input $\mathbf{u}$ and the barrier certificate $h(\mathbf{x})$. When an engineer specifies a safety constraint using raw geometric clearance $h(\mathbf{x}) = x_{\text{obstacle}} - x_{\text{robot}} \ge 0$, the commanded input (actuator torque or current) is separated from position by two time integrations:
$$\text{Actuation } u \xrightarrow{\int \frac{1}{m} dt} \text{Velocity } v \xrightarrow{\int dt} \text{Position } x$$
This two-step cascade defines relative degree $r = 2$. Differentiating spatial clearance once yields closing velocity ($\dot{h} = -v$), which contains zero control input ($L_g h(\mathbf{x}) = \text{JVP}(h, \mathbf{x}, g(\mathbf{x})) = \mathbf{0}$). Because the control authority JVP vanishes, motor torque has zero instantaneous leverage over the barrier's rate of decay. At the physical perimeter ($h = 0$), enforcing forward invariance $\dot{h} \ge -\kappa(0) = 0$ requires $-v \ge 0 \implies v \le 0$, demanding an instantaneous step in velocity that would require infinite deceleration and unbounded torque ($u = -\infty$). A barrier monitoring position alone registers danger only after momentum has already made contact inevitable.[^fn-math-cbf-degree]

[^fn-math-cbf-degree]: **Relative degree and inertia-aware barrier certificates**\index{Relative degree!Inertia-aware certificates}\index{Control barrier function!High-order}: When a safety barrier monitors position while the actuator commands torque, the control input is separated from the constraint by two time integrals ($r=2$). Enforcing a zero-order spatial barrier without embedding kinetic stopping distance produces an optimization problem with zero control authority on the boundary ($L_g h = \mathbf{0}$). A velocity-dependent barrier restores relative degree one ($r = 1$), supporting a conditional forward-invariance argument while braking remains feasible and the state, delay, and tracking margins hold; see @sec-appendix-control-cbf.

To restore nonzero control authority ($L_g h \neq \mathbf{0}$), the barrier certificate must incorporate kinetic energy and braking capability directly. For an approaching arm joint, let $D = d_{\text{tool}} / \ell$ be remaining angular clearance, $\omega > 0$ approach speed, $J \dot{\omega} = \tau + \tau_{\text{bias}}$, and $\alpha_{\text{net}}$ a validated lower bound on net available angular braking deceleration. The chapter uses the linear class-$\mathcal{K}$ choice $\kappa(h) = \gamma_{\text{cbf}} h$, with $\gamma_{\text{cbf}}>0$ a linear approach-rate gain. Define the **kinetic barrier certificate**:
$$h(D,\omega)=D-\frac{\omega^2}{2\alpha_{\text{net}}}.$$ {#eq-enforce-kinetic-barrier}
Differentiating $h(D,\omega)$ along the joint dynamics yields $\dot{h} = L_f h + L_g h\,\tau$, where $L_g h = -\frac{\omega}{J\alpha_{\text{net}}} \ne 0$ for approach speed $\omega > 0$. Because actuator torque $\tau$ appears directly in this first time derivative with a nonzero coefficient, the kinetic barrier achieves **relative degree one** ($r = 1$). Actuator torque now acts directly across the causal boundary. Enforcing the forward-invariance inequality $\dot{h} + \gamma_{\text{cbf}} h \ge 0$ isolates commanded torque into an explicit affine half-space constraint:[^fn-math-kinetic-derivation]
$$\tau\le-\tau_{\text{bias}}+J\alpha_{\text{net}}\left(\frac{\gamma_{\text{cbf}} h}{\omega}-1\right),\qquad -\tau_{\max}\le\tau\le\tau_{\max}.$$ {#eq-enforce-kinetic-torque}
This condition defines the linear half-space $\mathbf{a}(\mathbf{x})^\top \mathbf{u} \le b(\mathbf{x})$ solved by the control barrier function quadratic-program (CBF-QP) filter developed next, where the half-space normal and threshold are set by the Jacobian-vector products: $\mathbf{a}(\mathbf{x})^\top = -L_g h(\mathbf{x})$ and $b(\mathbf{x}) = L_f h(\mathbf{x}) + \gamma_{\text{cbf}} h(\mathbf{x})$ for the scalar gain used here.

[^fn-math-kinetic-derivation]: **Kinetic barrier directional derivative chain rule**: Evaluating $\dot{h}(D, \omega) = \frac{\partial h}{\partial D}\dot{D} + \frac{\partial h}{\partial \omega}\dot{\omega}$ with $\dot{D} = -\omega$ and $\dot{\omega} = (\tau + \tau_{\text{bias}})/J$ yields $\dot{h} = (-\omega - \frac{\omega\tau_{\text{bias}}}{J\alpha_{\text{net}}}) - \frac{\omega}{J\alpha_{\text{net}}}\tau = L_f h(D,\omega) + L_g h(D,\omega)\tau$. Substituting into $\dot{h} + \gamma_{\text{cbf}} h \ge 0$ and rearranging produces $\frac{\omega(\tau + \tau_{\text{bias}})}{J\alpha_{\text{net}}} \le \gamma_{\text{cbf}} h - \omega$. Multiplying by the positive factor $\frac{J\alpha_{\text{net}}}{\omega}$ and subtracting the bias yields @eq-enforce-kinetic-torque.

At standstill ($\omega=0$), the controller uses a separate no-approach and acceleration admission check; it does not divide by zero.[^fn-cbf-standstill-guard]

[^fn-cbf-standstill-guard]: **Standstill velocity thresholding**: In microcontroller firmware, floating-point evaluation of $\frac{\gamma_{\text{cbf}} h}{\omega}$ is explicitly guarded by a velocity threshold $\epsilon_{\text{vel}}$: when $|\omega| \le \epsilon_{\text{vel}}$, the kinetic barrier is bypassed in favor of a static acceleration or position-hold bound, preventing floating-point division by zero and NaN exceptions in the sub-millisecond loop.

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-kinetic-barrier
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ KINETIC BARRIER ON THE MACHINE'S DESCENDING ARM JOINT
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the loaded-arm paragraph immediately below (@eq-enforce-kinetic-torque).
# │ Goal:    evaluate the torque ceiling of the kinetic barrier at three clearances.
# │ Show:    alpha, h at 110 mm, the h = 0 clearance, and the braking torque demanded.
# │ How:     reuses the joint scenario of EnforcementAuthorityLoss (RM.arm torque).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_torque, check

class KineticBarrierArm:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    inertia = EnforcementAuthorityLoss.inertia  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    bias = EnforcementAuthorityLoss.bias  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    torque_limit = EnforcementAuthorityLoss.torque_limit  # category: datasheet
    speed = EnforcementAuthorityLoss.joint_speed  # rad/s; scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    radius = EnforcementAuthorityLoss.link_length  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    gamma = 10.0 / second  # scenario assumption; category: chosen (barrier gain)
    clear_far = 110 * millimeter  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative
    clear_near = 70 * millimeter  # scenario assumption; category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    alpha = ((torque_limit - bias) / inertia).to(1 / second**2)
    stop_angle = (speed**2 / (2 * alpha)).to("dimensionless")
    clear_zero = (radius * stop_angle).to(millimeter)
    angle_far = (clear_far / radius).to("dimensionless")
    h_far = angle_far - stop_angle
    h_near = (clear_near / radius).to("dimensionless") - stop_angle
    ceiling_far = (-bias + inertia * alpha * (gamma * h_far / speed - 1)).to(newton * meter)
    ceiling_zero = (-bias + inertia * alpha * (0 - 1)).to(newton * meter)
    ceiling_near = (-bias + inertia * alpha * (gamma * h_near / speed - 1)).to(newton * meter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(alpha.magnitude - 7.25) < 1e-9, "Net braking headroom gives 7.25 rad/s^2.")
    check(abs(ceiling_far.magnitude + 80.078125) < 1e-9, "At 110 mm the barrier demands at least 80.1 N·m of braking.")
    check(abs(ceiling_zero.magnitude + torque_limit.magnitude) < 1e-9, "At h = 0 the barrier demands the full peak torque.")
    check(-ceiling_near > torque_limit, "At 70 mm the demanded braking torque exceeds the joint's peak torque.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    alpha_str = fmt(alpha.magnitude, precision=2)
    gamma_str = fmt(gamma.magnitude, precision=0)
    angle_far_str = fmt(angle_far.magnitude, precision=4)
    h_far_str = fmt(h_far.magnitude, precision=4)
    clear_far_str = fmt_length(clear_far, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    clear_zero_str = fmt_length(clear_zero, unit=millimeter, precision=2)
    clear_near_str = fmt_length(clear_near, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    brake_far_str = fmt_torque(-ceiling_far, precision=1)
    brake_zero_str = fmt_torque(-ceiling_zero, precision=0)
    brake_near_str = fmt_torque(-ceiling_near, precision=1)
```

Carry the descending-arm scenario of @sec-enforcement-exhausted-authority into this barrier: $J=$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.inertia_str`, $\tau_{\text{bias}}=$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.bias_str` toward the station, $|\tau|\le$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.torque_limit_str`, $\alpha_{\text{net}}=(\tau_{\max}-\tau_{\text{bias}})/J=$ `{python} KineticBarrierArm.alpha_str` $\text{rad/s}^2$, $\ell=$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.link_length_str`, $\omega=$ `{python} EnforcementAuthorityLoss.joint_speed_str` $\text{rad/s}$, and $\gamma_{\text{cbf}}=$ `{python} KineticBarrierArm.gamma_str` $\text{s}^{-1}$. These are stated joint-level scenario inputs; the bias is not inferred from the payload mass alone. At `{python} KineticBarrierArm.clear_far_str` of tool clearance to the station surface, $D=$ `{python} KineticBarrierArm.angle_far_str` $\text{rad}$ and $h=$ `{python} KineticBarrierArm.h_far_str` $\text{rad}$, so @eq-enforce-kinetic-torque requires the joint to brake with at least `{python} KineticBarrierArm.brake_far_str`. At `{python} KineticBarrierArm.clear_zero_str`, $h=0$ and the requirement reaches `{python} KineticBarrierArm.brake_zero_str`, the joint's full peak torque. At `{python} KineticBarrierArm.clear_near_str`, it demands `{python} KineticBarrierArm.brake_near_str`, more than the joint can produce, so this state is already outside the modeled viable set. The enforcer must prevent entry into it; a fallback started there cannot restore the lost clearance.

A real machine realizes neither exact state feedback nor instantaneous torque. Stator current rise, bus jitter, and gearbox compliance delay and soften the corrective action, so the enforcer evaluates the barrier against a boundary inset by the worst-case stopping deficit they cause and intervenes earlier in the trajectory.

The kinetic barrier was not guessed. Its zero set is exactly the boundary of the states from which full braking still stops the joint before contact, the **viability kernel**\index{Viability kernel} of a braking double integrator, and its torque bound is compatible with the actuator. At $h = 0$ the bound of @eq-enforce-kinetic-torque equals $-\tau_{\max}$, and for $h > 0$ it is never more demanding than that, so a feasible command exists everywhere inside the set. That property, not the algebra of the derivative, is what makes it a valid barrier under input limits. The same construction applies to the base: $h_{\text{base}}(d, v) = d - [v\,\tau_{\text{delay}} + d_{\text{suffix}}(v) + \delta_{\text{loc}} + \delta_{\text{margin}} + \epsilon_{\text{track}}]$ is nonnegative exactly when @eq-enforce-stopping-envelope holds, so the stopping budget and the kinetic barrier are one idea written in two notations. The arm example drops the delay and allowance terms only to isolate the relative-degree argument. When the dynamics admit no closed-form kernel, **Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability**\index{Hamilton-Jacobi reachability} computes it numerically as the zero level set of a value function [@mitchell2005time; @bansal2017hamilton]. The resulting table can serve as the barrier, and its gradient supplies the same half-space (@sec-appendix-control-hj-reachability). The cost is grid size, which grows exponentially with state dimension, so HJ tables suit low-dimensional channels such as one joint or the base's longitudinal motion.

The barrier states which commands preserve the stop. It does not yet state what the permission path does with a proposal that fails it, whether to trim the proposal, refuse it, or keep the command already running, and that decision is what gives the barrier authority over the drive.

## Proposal Rejection Authority and State Invariants {#sec-enforcement-authority-refuse}

A trajectory chunk arrives from the application processor on schedule, properly framed, and bearing a fresh evidence timestamp, and one of its constituent joint setpoints would accelerate the arm directly into a steel rack upright. Nothing in the incoming packet payload marks that setpoint as erroneous. The permission path therefore grants zero executive authority to an incoming learned command until that proposal passes the configured state, input, freshness, and stopping-clearance checks. This is the concrete realization of the third bedrock law: **proposal is not permission** (principle \ref{pri-vol4-proposal-permission}), executed deterministically one millisecond tick at a time. The permission path does not assume that a learned proposal carries a stability, actuator-limit, or stopping guarantee; it treats the output as an advisory candidate.

The resident controller and output selector make refusal executable. The controller holds a response qualified for the current state; the selector admits a candidate, applies a feasible correction, or transfers control to that response. A new invalid replacement does not by itself invalidate the command already running. The previous command may continue only while its own evidence, lease, tracking bound, and stopping reservation remain valid.

Under this contract, the upstream neural policy never commands the plant directly. Instead, communication across the causal boundary operates through the chunk lease of @sec-nervous-cadences—a hardware-enforced dead-man permission that automatically lapses unless renewed by a fresh, valid proposal. The application processor transmits candidate control vectors as framed packets over the board-level link to the discrete safety MCU (@sec-placement-isolation-decisions); the two processors share no memory. The MCU's receiver, a direct memory access (DMA) transfer completed outside the tick's interrupt routine, checks each frame and copies it into the seqlock mailbox in the MCU's own memory (@sec-nervous-mailbox-exchanges).[^fn-hw-link-lease] Each proposal opens with the standardized proposal header (@sec-nervous-cadences), and the safety MCU checks its evidence timestamp and expiry deadline on each control cycle, adding the header's clock-synchronization error bound. A chunk arrives as $H$ waypoints (@sec-nervous-cadences), and admission checks all of them against reach, velocity, and stopping-reservation limits before any waypoint runs. The per-tick check then re-evaluates only the setpoint about to execute, against the live state. A projection on one tick does not rewrite the chunk's later waypoints; the intervention is reported upstream, and the proposer must replan from the corrected state rather than resume a chunk computed for a state the machine never reached.

If the proposal is fresh, the physical state remains inside the qualified stopping region, and tracking error satisfies $\|e(t)\| \le \epsilon_{\text{track}}$, the output selector permits the proposal (or its minimally projected variant $\mathbf{u}^*$) to drive the actuators. If the lease expires without renewal, tracking error breaches the certified bound, no command satisfies the current physical constraints, or the active command threatens physical boundaries beyond what projection can resolve, the output selector revokes permission and engages the baseline safety controller unilaterally.[^fn-hw-pwm-tripzone] The upstream neural policy is not consulted, does not negotiate, and possesses zero hardware mechanism to override the selector.

[^fn-hw-link-lease]: **Board-link transport timing**\index{Board-level link!proposal transport}\index{Black-channel principle!board link}: The link is treated as a black channel in the sense of the functional-safety fieldbus profiles [@iec61784-3-2021]. The header's checksum, sequence number, and lease detect what the link corrupts, repeats, loses, or delays, so its correctness is never assumed, but its timing still enters the budget. Serialization, DMA completion, and receive-interrupt latency age each newly admitted proposal and are charged to the dispatch-to-admission interval; their variation draws on the renewal-jitter allowance that the lease reserves (@sec-nervous-coupled-budget). Shared-memory messaging such as Linux RPMsg belongs to the shared-die placement that @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die evaluates, not to this machine.

[^fn-hw-pwm-tripzone]: **Hardware break circuits and PWM trip zones**\index{Hardware!Trip zones}\index{Pulse-width modulation!Hardware clamp}: A configured external timer break input such as `TIMx_BKIN` can force PWM outputs to a specified state without waiting for an interrupt. `EPWM_TZFRC` is a software force mechanism, not the external trip input. Output state and response time depend on the timer, gate drive, wiring, and qualification tests; the trip still needs a physically suitable stop path.

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-latch-filter
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE LATCH APPROACH AS THE FILTERING CASE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: the filter-vs.-veto paragraph immediately below; the record's
# │          approach-ceiling paragraph cites the same speeds.
# │ Goal:    give the chapter's first projection on the machine.
# │ Show:    the chunk policy's proposed approach and the target-ODD approach.
# │ How:     AISLE latch fields (the same ones EnforcementRecordMachine loads).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_velocity, check

AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class EnforcementLatchFilter:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_latch_high = AISLE.v_latch_high  # category: illustrative (policy's proposed approach)
    v_latch = AISLE.v_latch_approach  # category: chosen (target-ODD approach)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    speed_ratio = (v_latch_high / v_latch).to("dimensionless").magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v_latch_high.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.10) < 1e-9, "The policy proposes 0.10 m/s.")
    check(abs(v_latch.to(meter / second).magnitude - 0.03) < 1e-9, "The target-ODD approach is 0.03 m/s.")
    check(speed_ratio > 1.0, "The proposed approach is faster than the evidence covers.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_latch_high_str = fmt_velocity(v_latch_high, precision=2)
    v_latch_str = fmt_velocity(v_latch, precision=2)
```

When a proposal conflicts with physical constraints, the enforcer chooses between filtering and veto. Filtering applies when the proposal is structurally sound and a nearby admissible command still serves its intent. The spring-latched cage door that the arm opens supplies the case. The chunk policy's proposal to approach the door's strike plate at `{python} EnforcementLatchFilter.v_latch_high_str` is well formed, but the door zone admits only the `{python} EnforcementLatchFilter.v_latch_str` guarded approach of the target ODD, the one speed its demonstrations and trials cover (@sec-evaluation-logs). That ceiling marks where the evidence stops, not where the physics of the plate does. The enforcer therefore keeps the approach's direction and target and projects only its speed onto the `{python} EnforcementLatchFilter.v_latch_str` ceiling, a constraint that the least-change quadratic program\index{Quadratic programming} of @sec-enforcement-minimal-intervention enforces beside the half-spaces a Control Barrier Function\index{Control barrier function} derives.

Filtering must respect momentum as well as position, because the actuators must still be able to stop the machine before clearance vanishes (@sec-enforcement-safe-sets-conditional-permission). For the latch example, speed projection preserves the target and direction. In a coupled torque filter, a correction may change the task-space path; it is permissible only when the revised motion remains admissible and continuity constraints hold. A structurally invalid proposal, such as a discontinuous jump in commanded position, an acceleration beyond the available torque, or a trajectory aimed into an immovable obstacle, indicates that perception or inference has entered an unmodeled failure mode, and projecting it onto the nearest safe boundary would execute a motion unrelated to any task intent. The enforcer vetoes such a replacement. It retains the active command only while that command passes its own checks; otherwise the selector transfers authority to a feasible local fallback.

Filtering and veto both happen at runtime, and training the policy cannot replace either. As @sec-boundary-fallacies-pitfalls argues, penalty terms and barrier losses shape the distribution a policy learns but do not bound what the deployed policy emits. The **statistical safety fallacy**\index{Statistical safety fallacy} is to treat a bound on expected violation cost as a bound on every deployed trajectory. A constrained reinforcement learning\index{Constrained reinforcement learning} objective such as $\mathbb{E}[\text{cost}] \le \delta$ alone permits uneven outcomes across episodes. Neural-network verification can establish output bounds on a stated input set [@katz2017reluplex], and closed-loop verification can combine those with plant models. Neither automatically covers friction, sensing, timing, or actuator behavior outside its assumptions. The permission path therefore checks each candidate at its actuation boundary whatever objective trained the proposer, and when the proposal is safe, the check is transparent and the learned competence passes to the drive unchanged.

The chunk lease, `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.lease_ms_str` on this machine, also keeps the enforcer's authority when the upstream host stalls. A separate `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.heartbeat_rate_hz_str` $\text{Hz}$ host heartbeat has a `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.heartbeat_timeout_ms_str` silence timeout. The `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.loop_rate_str` MCU loop feeds its own `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.self_watchdog_ms_str` self-watchdog only after a successful cycle; a separate external trip covers MCU failure. At a host-heartbeat or chunk-lease timeout the functioning MCU revokes the proposal and executes a resident, state-matched fallback from the Fallback Ladder, provided the reserved clearance and available braking still suffice. On the warehouse mobile manipulator, if a proposer renews its lease and then stalls, the brake still begins within `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.renewal_to_onset_ms_str` of the last valid renewal. This lease-expiry case assumes the separate heartbeat remains live while fresh admissible proposals stop arriving; a total host stall triggers the `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.heartbeat_timeout_ms_str` heartbeat timeout earlier. When the danger is a person stepping out at the rack end, the age of the frame that first showed that person adds to the renewal-to-onset delay, and @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes carries the sum into the admission check. Enforcing the lease at the drive, rather than trusting the host to withdraw its own proposal, is what bounds the delay at all.

Severing upstream authority requires a defined physical response at the lowest hardware interface. The zero-command floor\index{Zero-command floor} is the configured response when active software control disappears, and writing zero to a drive produces different mechanics on different actuators. Zero current in a low-friction direct drive lets a gravity-loaded arm descend unless a separate restraint carries the load, while zero velocity in a stiff position loop can request a large transient. @Sec-body-power-integrity describes the three unpowered states a drive can fall into (free coasting, phase-short dynamic braking\index{Dynamic braking}, or a spring-applied brake); the selected response must match the state and the hardware that remains available.

Refusal is a steady-state decision, not only an emergency exception. The checks above must remain executable when the proposer fails, and the selected response must retain sensing, braking authority, and clearance. When those premises do hold, a feasible correction can preserve the learned proposal's useful intent.

## The Minimal Intervention Principle and Optimization Filters {#sec-enforcement-minimal-intervention}

The arm can approach the latch too quickly while still proposing a useful target and direction. Rejecting every such proposal would discard useful learned behavior; accepting it would exceed the permitted approach. The **minimal intervention principle**\index{Minimal intervention} instead preserves a proposal when it is admissible and chooses the smallest feasible correction when it is not. A correction still has to satisfy the physical constraints and finish before the permission deadline.

The resulting **safety shield**\index{Safety shield}\index{Minimal-intervention QP projection (safety shield)} preserves useful task progress within the physical limits. For the torque forbidden by @eq-enforce-kinetic-torque, the correction should remove only the constraint violation; replacing every near-boundary command with a stop would discard admissible learned behavior.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Nominal trajectory setpoints and feedforward torques are synthesized by the planner in @sec-planning-goal-to-trajectory.
:::

For the already-derived torque half-space, the enforcer solves a constrained least-change problem [@ames2016control]. The tracker supplies the nominal effort; the barrier and actuator limits constrain the result. A combined tracking-and-barrier optimization can instead soften tracking convergence when the objectives conflict, as derived in @sec-appendix-control-lyapunov. That additional controller design is not required to implement the filter here:[^fn-hw-cortex-cycles]
$$\min_{\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^m} \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}_{\text{nom}}\|^2 \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \mathbf{a}(\mathbf{x})^\top \mathbf{u} \le b(\mathbf{x}), \quad \mathbf{u}_{\min} \le \mathbf{u} \le \mathbf{u}_{\max}$$ {#eq-enforce-cbf-qp}
where the half-space normal and threshold are defined by the directional derivatives $\mathbf{a}(\mathbf{x})^\top = -L_g h(\mathbf{x})$ and $b(\mathbf{x}) = L_f h(\mathbf{x}) + \kappa(h(\mathbf{x}))$ derived in @sec-enforcement-kinetic-barrier-certificates,[^fn-math-cbf-lie] matching the single-axis torque constraint of @eq-enforce-kinetic-torque, and $[\mathbf{u}_{\min}, \mathbf{u}_{\max}]$ represents the verified actuator torque envelope. The selected implementation allocates $150\,\mu\text{s}$ to this solve. Dedicated memory and a fixed iteration cap support that target; qualification must establish completion or a timely fallback under the admitted constraint set.

[^fn-math-cbf-lie]: **Control barrier functions and directional derivatives**\index{Control barrier function!Lie derivatives}\index{Nonlinear control!Lie derivatives}: For a general control-affine system $\dot{\mathbf{x}} = f(\mathbf{x}) + g(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u}$, the directional time derivative of a scalar barrier function $h(\mathbf{x})$ evaluates to $\dot{h}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}) = \nabla h(\mathbf{x}) \cdot f(\mathbf{x}) + \nabla h(\mathbf{x}) \cdot g(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u} = L_f h(\mathbf{x}) + L_g h(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u}$. Here $L_f h(\mathbf{x}) \triangleq \nabla h(\mathbf{x}) \cdot f(\mathbf{x})$ denotes the directional derivative along unforced system drift, while $L_g h(\mathbf{x}) \triangleq \nabla h(\mathbf{x}) \cdot g(\mathbf{x})$ denotes the directional derivative along control input (conventionally termed Lie derivatives). When $L_g h(\mathbf{x}) \neq \mathbf{0}$, the boundary has relative degree one ($r = 1$), yielding an instantaneous affine constraint on commanded torque: $L_f h(\mathbf{x}) + L_g h(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u} \ge -\kappa(h(\mathbf{x}))$. If $L_g h(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}$, the relative degree is two or higher, requiring higher-order barrier formulations; see @sec-appendix-control-cbf.

[^fn-hw-cortex-cycles]: **Worst-case execution time and active-set QP complexity**\index{Quadratic programming!Worst-case execution time}\index{Worst-case execution time!Active-set QP}: A fixed iteration cap bounds the number of solver steps, not their duration. A complete timing bound must also cover each step's arithmetic, memory access, interrupts, and output transfer under admitted interference. Static arrays remove dynamic-allocation variability; qualified memory and bus service and a surviving timeout response remain necessary.

::: {#dfn-enforcement-control-barrier-function-cbf-qp .callout-definition title="Control barrier function safety filter"}

***Control barrier function safety filter***\index{Control barrier function!definition}\index{CBF-QP safety filter!definition} is the constrained optimization filter that projects unverified nominal control proposals $\mathbf{u}_{\text{nom}}$ onto an admissible input set whose constraints preserve the state set $\mathcal{C} = \{\mathbf{x} \mid h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0\}$ under the stated assumptions, by solving the quadratic program:
$$\min_{\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^m} \frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}_{\text{nom}}\|^2 \quad \text{s.t.} \quad L_f h(\mathbf{x}) + L_g h(\mathbf{x}) \mathbf{u} \ge -\kappa(h(\mathbf{x})), \quad \mathbf{u}_{\min} \le \mathbf{u} \le \mathbf{u}_{\max}$$
that enforces linear braking half-space constraints ($L_f h(\mathbf{x}) + L_g h(\mathbf{x}) \mathbf{u} \ge -\kappa(h(\mathbf{x}))$), leaving candidate inputs that satisfy the safe boundary untouched and minimally projecting violating inputs in control space within the implementation's qualified execution budget.

1.  **Significance**: A CBF-QP filter separates high-level policy innovation from low-level safety enforcement. The learned model is free to explore complex manipulation or navigation strategies, while the deterministic enforcer can preserve a validated viable set while its physical assumptions remain true.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike a heuristic clamp that saturates control channels independently (destroying multi-axis coordination), a CBF-QP filter performs an optimal orthogonal projection in control space, minimizing the chosen torque-space distance; it does not automatically preserve a Cartesian path.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Formulating barrier constraints using raw geometric coordinates without accounting for relative degree ($r = 2$) or braking inertia. If the barrier does not incorporate stopping distance ($\Delta d_{\text{stop}} = v\,\tau_{\text{delay}} + v^2 / 2a_{\text{brake}}$), the filter intervenes too late, after the vehicle's momentum has already made a boundary collision inevitable.

:::

### Closed-form quadratic programming and torque projection {#sec-enforcement-qp-projection}

A single active barrier admits a closed-form projection when the projected command also lies inside the actuator bounds. If a bound becomes active, the enforcer must solve for the intersection rather than project onto the barrier and clamp afterward.

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforce-cbf-qp-projection
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
import math
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_cbf_qp_orthogonal_projection
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, check

class CBFQPProjection:
    u_nom = [3.5, 3.0]  # N·m; category: illustrative (abstract proposal)
    a_vec = [2.0, 1.0]  # category: illustrative (abstract half-space normal)
    b_scalar = 5.0  # N·m; category: illustrative (abstract threshold)
    u_clip = [2.0, 3.0]  # N·m; category: illustrative (per-axis clamp for contrast)
    u_lim = 5.0  # N·m; category: illustrative (symmetric per-joint actuator limit)

    res = calc_cbf_qp_orthogonal_projection(u_nom, a_vec, b_scalar)
    u_proj = res["u_projected"]
    lambda_star = res["lambda_star"]
    correction_norm = res["correction_norm"]

    a_dot_u_nom = a_vec[0] * u_nom[0] + a_vec[1] * u_nom[1]
    breach = a_dot_u_nom - b_scalar
    a_dot_u_clip = a_vec[0] * u_clip[0] + a_vec[1] * u_clip[1]
    clip_penetration = a_dot_u_clip - b_scalar

    theta_nom_deg = math.degrees(math.atan2(u_nom[1], u_nom[0]))
    theta_clip_deg = math.degrees(math.atan2(u_clip[1], u_clip[0]))
    skew_deg = theta_clip_deg - theta_nom_deg

    check(abs(u_proj[0]) <= u_lim and abs(u_proj[1]) <= u_lim, "The projected command stays within the joint limits.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    u_nom_1_str = fmt(u_nom[0], precision=1)
    u_nom_2_str = fmt(u_nom[1], precision=0)
    a_1_str = fmt(a_vec[0], precision=0)
    a_2_str = fmt(a_vec[1], precision=0)
    b_str = fmt(b_scalar, precision=0)
    u_lim_str = fmt(u_lim, precision=0)

    a_dot_u_nom_str = fmt(a_dot_u_nom, precision=0)
    breach_str = fmt(breach, precision=0)
    lambda_star_str = fmt(lambda_star, precision=0)
    u_proj_1_str = fmt(u_proj[0], precision=1)
    u_proj_2_str = fmt(u_proj[1], precision=0)
    correction_norm_str = fmt(correction_norm, precision=3)

    u_clip_1_str = fmt(u_clip[0], precision=0)
    u_clip_2_str = fmt(u_clip[1], precision=0)
    a_dot_u_clip_str = fmt(a_dot_u_clip, precision=0)
    clip_penetration_str = fmt(clip_penetration, precision=0)
    theta_nom_deg_str = fmt(theta_nom_deg, precision=1)
    theta_clip_deg_str = fmt(theta_clip_deg, precision=1)
    skew_deg_str = fmt(skew_deg, precision=1)
```

For a nonzero constraint normal and inactive actuator bounds, the single barrier constraint $\mathbf{a}^\top \mathbf{u} \le b$ in @eq-enforce-cbf-qp admits the closed-form projection derived in @sec-appendix-control-cbf-qp:
$$\mathbf{u}^* = \mathbf{u}_{\text{nom}} - \lambda^* \mathbf{a}, \qquad \lambda^* = \max\left(0, \frac{\mathbf{a}^\top \mathbf{u}_{\text{nom}} - b}{\|\mathbf{a}\|^2}\right)$$ {#eq-enforce-cbf-projection}
where the optimal dual multiplier $\lambda^* \ge 0$ is zero whenever the nominal proposal is safe ($\mathbf{a}^\top \mathbf{u}_{\text{nom}} \le b$), leaving $\mathbf{u}^* = \mathbf{u}_{\text{nom}}$, and strictly positive when the proposal breaches the boundary ($\mathbf{a}^\top \mathbf{u}_{\text{nom}} > b$), scaling the minimal intervention vector $\Delta \mathbf{u} = -\lambda^* \mathbf{a}$ to project $\mathbf{u}^*$ orthogonally onto the safe half-space boundary $\mathbf{a}^\top \mathbf{u} = b$.

The projection arithmetic is clearest on a two-axis manipulator with illustrative values. Its tracker, following setpoints from an unconstrained neural policy, computes nominal joint torques $\mathbf{u}_{\text{nom}} = [$ `{python} CBFQPProjection.u_nom_1_str`, `{python} CBFQPProjection.u_nom_2_str` $]^\top\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$. Suppose an abstract safety half-space has already been derived and validated, $\mathbf{a}^\top \mathbf{u} \le b$ with $\mathbf{a} = [$ `{python} CBFQPProjection.a_1_str`, `{python} CBFQPProjection.a_2_str` $]^\top$ and $b =$ `{python} CBFQPProjection.b_str` $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$, with per-joint actuator limits of $\pm$`{python} CBFQPProjection.u_lim_str` $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$. The candidate gives $\mathbf{a}^\top \mathbf{u}_{\text{nom}} =$ `{python} CBFQPProjection.a_dot_u_nom_str` $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ and breaches the boundary by `{python} CBFQPProjection.breach_str` $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$.

By @eq-enforce-cbf-projection, $\lambda^* =$ `{python} CBFQPProjection.lambda_star_str`, and the minimal-intervention command is $\mathbf{u}^* = [$ `{python} CBFQPProjection.u_proj_1_str`, `{python} CBFQPProjection.u_proj_2_str` $]^\top\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, which meets the half-space exactly while both joints stay within their limits, with an intervention norm of `{python} CBFQPProjection.correction_norm_str` $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$.

Per-axis clamping shows why the projection is needed. Clamping Joint 1 to `{python} CBFQPProjection.u_clip_1_str` $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ while passing Joint 2 at `{python} CBFQPProjection.u_clip_2_str` $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ gives $\mathbf{a}^\top \mathbf{u}_{\text{clip}} =$ `{python} CBFQPProjection.a_dot_u_clip_str` $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$, still `{python} CBFQPProjection.clip_penetration_str` $\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$ outside the constraint, and it skews the torque vector from `{python} CBFQPProjection.theta_nom_deg_str`$^\circ$ to `{python} CBFQPProjection.theta_clip_deg_str`$^\circ$. The clamp therefore both violates the constraint and distorts the command. The projection satisfies the constraint with the smallest possible torque change, although it too rotates the torque vector, so the end-effector path still needs a check against the coupled plant model.

This geometric behavior exposes the distinction between **torque-space and task-space minimal intervention**\index{Minimal intervention!torque vs. task space}: an orthogonal projection $\mathbf{u}^* = \mathbf{u}_{\text{nom}} + \Delta \mathbf{u}$ minimizes joint effort deviation $\|\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}_{\text{nom}}\|^2$, which redistributes multi-axis joint torques and rotates the net Cartesian wrench. While a feasible projection can preserve the safe set $\mathcal{C}$ under the stated model and timing assumptions, it deflects the end-effector trajectory and may arrest task progress. If the upstream neural policy continues emitting unprojected nominal setpoints without awareness of the intervention, the robot can chatter or stall at the boundary. The downstream enforcer must therefore stream the intervention vector $\Delta \mathbf{u}$ back to the application processor as a telemetry signal, notifying the high-level planner to re-plan around the newly active physical constraint.

@Fig-12-cbf-safety-filter shows both views. In state space (panel a), proposals that would cross the barrier are deflected along the inset boundary $\partial \mathcal{C}$; in control space (panel b), the enforcer projects $\mathbf{u}_{\text{nom}}$ onto the half-space $\mathbf{a}^\top \mathbf{u} \le b$, while the independently clamped vector stays outside it.

::: {#fig-12-cbf-safety-filter fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Kinetic barrier and torque projection**: Panel (a) schematically shows a velocity-dependent viable boundary inset from geometric clearance; the raw distance alone has relative degree two for torque. Panel (b) illustrates Euclidean projection onto a supplied torque half-space. The $[2,1]$ normal and $5\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ threshold are abstract arithmetic inputs, not coefficients derived from the arm example." fig-alt="Two panels: a schematic inset stopping boundary in state space, and a two-axis torque plane in which a nominal command is projected onto a feasible half-space while a per-axis clamped command remains outside it."}
![](images/svg/fig12_cbf_safety_filter.svg){width="100%"}
:::

Filter choice joins a mathematical condition to a measured execution budget and the machine's available braking authority. As summarized in @tbl-12-safety-filter-architectures, architectural choices differ in their handling of relative degree, solver worst-case execution time (WCET), forward invariance guarantees, and directional fidelity. Independent clamping can miss coupled constraints; a CBF-QP can enforce a derived half-space if it is feasible and finishes within the verified cycle. Predictive filters [@wabersich2021predictive] trade a longer horizon for configuration-dependent compute cost.

The rows are members of one family rather than rival techniques [@hsu2024safetyfilter]. Each filter monitors a candidate against a **fallback policy**\index{Fallback policy!safety filter} that is known to keep the machine safe, and intervenes when the candidate would leave the set from which that fallback still works. Filters differ in how they intervene. A **least-restrictive**\index{Safety filter!least-restrictive} filter passes the proposal untouched until the boundary and then switches to the fallback, which is simple but chatters at the boundary. A smooth filter such as the CBF-QP blends a correction in before the boundary. This chapter's enforcer uses both. Admitting a trajectory only with a matched stop suffix, and holding a state-matched fallback for every reachable state, is a **backup-set filter**\index{Backup-set filter}: safety is certified by rolling the fallback forward from the proposed state [@gurriet2018online; @chen2021backup]. The per-tick CBF-QP is the smooth local filter layered on it. HJ reachability [@fisac2019general] supplies the value function for the table row that replaces a closed-form barrier with a precomputed one.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{26\baselineskip}
```

| Filter                         | Input and condition                                                                      | What it can establish                                                   | Main validation task                                                                                                         |
|:-------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Independent torque clamp       | Each axis checked separately                                                             | Hardware amplitude limit, not coupled stopping clearance                | Test coupled wrench and stopping behavior                                                                                    |
| First-order CBF-QP             | Barrier whose first derivative contains the input                                        | Conditional invariance from a viable initial state                      | Validate model, feasible torque set, and cycle bound                                                                         |
| Kinetic / higher-order barrier | Position constraint with speed and braking authority included                            | Conditional stopping margin before geometric contact                    | Bound bias torque, delay, estimate error, and discretization                                                                 |
| Energy tank / passivity filter | State $E_{\text{tank}}$, power balance $\dot{E}_{\text{tank}}$, force $F_{\text{limit}}$ | Conditional energy bound; force requires a separately qualified channel | Bound force-sensor bias, calibrate virtual damping matrix $\mathbf{D}_{\text{virt}}$, and set reserve floor $E_{\text{min}}$ |
| HJ value-function filter       | Precomputed value function over a gridded state space                                    | Containment for the modeled region                                      | Verify grid coverage, interpolation error, and disturbance bounds                                                            |
| Predictive safety filter       | Finite-horizon trajectory and terminal set                                               | Recursive feasibility only under terminal and timing assumptions        | Bound full solve time and fallback on timeout                                                                                |

: **Safety-filter decisions**: A filter's physical claim depends on the chosen barrier and validated plant, not on the algorithm name. Nominal solve measurements are not worst-case deadlines. {#tbl-12-safety-filter-architectures tbl-colwidths="[20,26,28,26]"}

Operating near an active safe-set boundary can produce chattering. If a learned policy repeatedly proposes an unsafe command, sampled enforcement may switch the active constraint across successive `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.tick_ms_str` ticks. Depending on the plant and controller, rapid torque changes can excite a structural mode or increase motor heating and transmission wear. A tested boundary layer or hysteresis can reduce switching, but its added tracking error must fit inside the validated stopping margin.

The intervention vector $\Delta u = u^* - u_{\text{nom}}$ also measures upstream policy health. A rising intervention frequency or magnitude can indicate proposal drift, a changed task, or a changed plant. Normal filtering can also preserve successful whole-machine service while reducing unassisted proposer autonomy; the log must distinguish these outcomes rather than count every correction as a task failure. Summed over an illustrative rolling window of $W = 500\text{ ms}$ as $\sum_{k} \|u_k^* - u_{\text{nom}, k}\| \Delta t$, the metric lets the permission path flag divergence for logging or operator notification while the per-tick limits still protect the plant.

### Intentional contact and in-contact energy barriers {#sec-enforcement-intentional-contact}

This kinetic barrier operates under an essential premise: the robot's objective is to avoid collision ($D > 0$). In manipulation, grasping, and assembly, that premise inverts: the task requires intentional physical contact ($D = 0$). If an arm closing on a workbench to grasp a workpiece or insert a pin evaluates @eq-enforce-kinetic-barrier at $D = 0$, the condition $h(0, \omega) = -\omega^2 / (2\alpha_{\text{net}}) \ge 0$ admits only $\omega = 0$. This barrier can admit arrival at contact with zero approach speed. It does not describe the subsequent force-controlled interaction, where geometric separation no longer supplies the relevant margin. On the warehouse mobile manipulator that interaction is the cage door: once the gripper meets the strike plate at the guarded approach, the arm must push against the latch spring, and the margin that matters is the energy and force it delivers there.

Enforcing safety during intentional contact requires transitioning from a **spatial clearance barrier** to an **energetic passivity barrier**\index{Passivity observer!contact safety}\index{Energy tank!contact barrier function}. When physical clearance is zero ($D_{\text{clear}} = 0$), safety cannot mean zero velocity; it means bounding mechanical energy exchange and normal contact force $F_n$. A controller in physical contact interacts with an unmodeled, potentially stiff environment. If tracking errors or neural policy oscillations pump unmeasured energy into the interface, the closed-loop system undergoes contact chattering, limit cycles, or high-force impact spikes that damage both the workpiece and the robot's transmission.

To bound active energy exchange, the enforcer augments the controller state with an **energy tank** $E_{\text{tank}}(t)$ [@ferraguti2013tank; @hogan1985impedance]. The tank is a software work ledger, not a source of recovered heat. In this contact formulation, $\mathbf{u}$ denotes the active torque component excluding damping, and the total controller torque is $\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{D}_{\text{virt}}\dot{\mathbf{q}}$. The damping term can credit the ledger only to the extent that the actuator actually realizes the corresponding dissipative work. Using total torque in the debit while also crediting damping would count the same dissipation twice. With those components separated, the modeled balance is:
$$\dot{E}_{\text{tank}} = \dot{\mathbf{q}}^\top \mathbf{D}_{\text{virt}}\,\dot{\mathbf{q}} - \mathbf{u}^\top \dot{\mathbf{q}}$$ {#eq-enforce-energy-tank}
where $\dot{\mathbf{q}}^\top \mathbf{D}_{\text{virt}}\,\dot{\mathbf{q}} \ge 0$ is the dissipative power credited under qualified torque tracking and $\mathbf{u}^\top \dot{\mathbf{q}}$ is active mechanical power. Saturation, delay, or tracking error requires conservative bounds on realized work rather than credit for an unrealized damping request. The enforcer then defines the energy-tank barrier certificate of @eq-enforce-energy-cbf:
$$h_{\text{energy}}(\mathbf{x}, E_{\text{tank}}) = E_{\text{tank}} - E_{\text{min}} \ge 0$$ {#eq-enforce-energy-cbf}
where $E_{\text{min}} > 0$ is a reserved baseline. Combined with a hard contact-force limit $h_{\text{force}}(\mathbf{F}_{\text{contact}}) = F_{\text{limit}} - \|\mathbf{F}_{\text{contact}}\| \ge 0$, the enforcer establishes the in-contact viable set $\mathcal{C}_{\text{contact}}$. While $E_{\text{tank}} > E_{\text{min}}$ and $\|\mathbf{F}_{\text{contact}}\| < F_{\text{limit}}$, candidate neural actions are admitted to perform manipulation. If the task consumes the allocated energy budget ($E_{\text{tank}} \to E_{\text{min}}$) or contact force approaches $F_{\text{limit}}$, the barrier filter clamps active energy injection ($\mathbf{u}^\top \dot{\mathbf{q}} \le 0$), restricting active work under the modeled power balance. This energy constraint does not by itself bound contact force: a passive interaction with a stiff surface can still produce a large force. The force channel needs its own sensing-error, response-delay, and actuator bounds before the combined constraints can justify continued contact.

For a contact command, integrating the work balance in @eq-enforce-energy-tank over one control interval $\Delta t$ supplies the energy allowance for the same least-change decision. Let $E_0\ge E_{\min}$ be the current tank level, $P_d$ a conservative lower bound on damping power actually realized, and $v_c>0$ a bounded contact-direction speed held for this simplified interval. The spendable work is $E_0-E_{\min}+P_d\Delta t$. A proposed constant force $F_{\mathrm{nom}}\ge0$ debits $F_{\mathrm{nom}}v_c\Delta t$, so the energy allowance caps force at $F_E=(E_0-E_{\min}+P_d\Delta t)/(v_c\Delta t)$. Let $F_{\mathrm{cap}}$ be the smaller of the deliverable force and the contact-force ceiling after sensing and delay allowances. Under these stipulated scalar conditions, the admitted command is $F^*=\min(F_{\mathrm{nom}},F_E,F_{\mathrm{cap}})$. Its debit leaves $E_1=E_0+P_d\Delta t-F^*v_c\Delta t\ge E_{\min}$ and its force stays below the independent cap. The controller can therefore continue useful contact with a reduced force instead of abandoning the task. At the reserve with no credited damping, no positive active work is admitted. Zero speed requires a separate force check rather than division by speed, and delayed or uncertain power requires conservative work bounds over the interval.

The containment claim provided by both spatial and energetic barrier calculations is strictly conditional. A forward-invariance claim requires a feasible barrier and the following bounded conditions; the list is necessary for this design, not an exhaustive if-and-only-if test:

1. **Model Fidelity:** The nominal plant dynamics $f(x)$ and $g(x)$ must capture the true system dynamics within a certified parameter error bound.
2. **Disturbance Bounds:** External forces and unmodeled friction acting on the mass must remain strictly within the modeled disturbance envelope $|d(t)| \le d_{\max}$.
3. **Actuation Authority:** Physical actuators must possess sufficient voltage, current, and thermal headroom to realize the commanded corrective force without saturation ($u^* \in [u_{\min}, u_{\max}]$).
4. **Solver Determinism:** The optimization solver or projection algorithm must terminate strictly within its allocated execution budget ($T_{\text{solve}} \le T_{\text{budget}} < T_{\text{loop}}$).
5. **Discretization Invariance:** The discrete sampling interval $T_{\text{ctrl}}$ must be sufficiently small that inter-sample state drift does not breach the continuous-time invariance boundary.

Each condition maps to a budget. Model fidelity and disturbance bounds come from system identification and load testing on the bench, actuation authority from dynamometer curves and thermal limits (@sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles), solver determinism from static worst-case execution time analysis on the MCU, and discretization from the loop period, which at $T_{\text{ctrl}} =$ `{python} EnforcementLeaseStop.tick_ms_str` must keep the zero-order-hold drift between samples to a fraction of $\delta_{\text{margin}}$.

A condition that no detector watches is an assumption, so the permission path attaches one to each: a **disturbance observer**\index{Disturbance observer} compares predicted with measured acceleration on every cycle, inverter status registers and current shunts report actuator saturation\index{Actuator saturation}, a hardware watchdog\index{Hardware watchdog} and cycle counter time the solver against its deadline, and timestamp counters on the sensor bus catch jitter and missed samples.

When a detector invalidates a premise, the enforcer cannot restore permission by substituting optimistic parameters. It selects a response whose sensing, effort, and clearance premises survive, as developed in @sec-enforcement-fallback-ladder. Both the free-space projection and contact decision must finish before the physical margin reserved for computation is spent.

### Deterministic execution timing and the sub-millisecond loop {#sec-enforcement-loop-budget}

A correct barrier calculation delivered after the permission deadline cannot protect the margin reserved for that deadline. The whole cycle must therefore have a bounded execution time, including state acquisition and the final drive transfer. A real-time operating system can reduce scheduling delays, but its name does not establish a bound on shared-memory or peripheral interference. The permission path's implementation must be qualified under the competing workloads that can delay it.

The declared cycle allocation below is a timing requirement carried into loaded placement tests. It is not a measured trace or a platform-independent solver guarantee.

```{python}
#| label: calc-enforcement-cycle-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌── LOAD: declared enforcer cycle budget ────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import Embodied
from mlsysim.core.units import microsecond, millisecond
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, check

class EnforcementCycleBudget:
    scenario = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle
    wcet = scenario.enforcer_wcet  # category: chosen (declared, not measured)
    deadline = scenario.enforcer_deadline  # category: chosen
    tick = scenario.t_tick  # category: chosen
    unloaded = scenario.enforcer_unloaded  # category: illustrative (unloaded observed cycle)
    acquisition = 30 * microsecond  # category: chosen (sub-budget; with the proposal check it covers the unloaded 40 us read in Ch13)
    proposal_lease = 15 * microsecond  # category: chosen (sub-budget)
    tracking = 10 * microsecond  # category: chosen (sub-budget)
```
